title: Ancient package
context: An 1896 X-ray of something wrapped up tight for a very, very long time.
question: What is it?

img.file: Mummy bird from an Egyptian tomb (1896).png
img.author: Charles Thurstan Holland (1896)
img.alt: A grey, wrapped bundle showing a bird's skull, wings and legs inside.

hints: It came out of an ancient Egyptian tomb.
Look for the skull, wings and legs under the wrapping.
why: One of the earliest X-rays of an ancient object: a mummified bird from an Egyptian tomb, X-rayed in Liverpool in October 1896.
pearl: Ancient Egyptians mummified millions of birds, especially ibises, as offerings to their gods. This X-ray was taken less than a year after X-rays were discovered.

title: Twinkle twinkle
context: Five arms, a lacy skeleton and not a single bone you'd recognise.
question: What is it?

img.author: Nevit Dilmen
img.alt: A five-armed star shape with a fine net-like skeleton, glowing on black.

hints: It lives in rock pools and on the sea floor.
It can regrow a lost arm.
why: An X-ray of a starfish, showing the mesh of tiny chalky plates that makes up its skeleton.
pearl: Starfish have no brain. Most have a simple eye at the tip of each arm.

title: Look closer
context: Two ovals joined by a thin bridge, X-rayed in Frankfurt in 1896.
question: What is it?

img.author: Walter König (1896)
img.alt: An old sepia X-ray of a pair of oval spectacles with thin frames.

hints: You'd wear them on your face.
They help you see.
why: An X-ray of a pair of glasses taken in Frankfurt, Germany, in 1896. The metal frame stops X-rays better than the glass lenses.
pearl: This X-ray was made months after X-rays were discovered, and it took three minutes. Today an airport scanner takes a fraction of a second.

title: Pond life
context: A chunky fish with a big air bladder showing as a dark pocket.
question: What is it?

img.author: Florian Elias Rieser
img.alt: A fish skeleton with a large dark air pocket in its body.

hints: It loves muddy rivers and lakes.
Koi are a fancy, colourful version.
why: An X-ray of a common carp. The dark pocket is its swim bladder, which helps it float.
pearl: Goldfish and koi are both close relatives of the common carp, and carp can live for decades.

title: Armour plated
context: Two big claws, a segmented tail and no bones at all. X-rayed in 1896.
question: What is it?

img.author: Walter König (1896)
img.alt: A sepia X-ray of a clawed crustacean with a segmented tail.

hints: It lives in the sea.
It turns red when it's cooked.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a lobster-like crustacean from Frankfurt's Senckenberg Museum.
pearl: Lobsters have blue blood. It uses copper, not iron, to carry oxygen.

title: Say cheese
context: A small deep-sea fish with a huge head and a terrifying grin.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A small fish skeleton with a big head and long teeth.

hints: It lives in the dark, deep ocean.
Its name says it all.
why: An X-ray of a fangtooth from the Bear Seamount in the Atlantic Ocean.
pearl: Compared with its body size, the fangtooth has some of the largest teeth of any fish.

title: Gone fishing
context: A lumpy fish with a huge mouth and something like a tiny rod on its head.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A lumpy fish skeleton with a large mouth and a thin spine on its head.

hints: It uses a lure to catch its dinner.
It's named after a hopping amphibian.
why: An X-ray of a scarlet frogfish from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Frogfish dangle a fleshy lure on a 'fishing rod' fin, then gulp prey in a split second with their enormous mouths.

title: Big mouth
context: A long whip of a tail and a mouth that's mostly... mouth.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A long thin fish with a huge hinged jaw and a whip-like tail.

hints: It lives in the deep sea.
Its other name is the pelican eel.
why: An X-ray of a gulper eel, also called a pelican eel, from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: A gulper eel's huge, loose jaw works like a pelican's pouch, scooping up prey along with a mouthful of water.

title: Flat out
context: A fish shaped like a flat oval, with fins frilling all the way round.
question: What is it?

img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: A flat oval fish skeleton with fins along both edges.

hints: It lies on its side on the sea floor.
Both its eyes end up on the same side of its head.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a sole, a flatfish, from one of the first X-ray photo books.
pearl: Baby flatfish look like normal fish. As they grow, one eye slowly moves across to the other side of the head.

title: Jump scare
context: Two little skeletons with very long back legs and no tail.
question: What is it?

img.file: Frösche in Bauch und Rückenlage MET DP262483.jpg
img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: Two frog skeletons with long hind legs, one belly up and one belly down.

hints: They are amphibians.
They say 'ribbit' in cartoons.
why: An 1896 X-ray of two frogs, one lying on its back and one on its front.
pearl: Frogs use their eyes to help them swallow: they pull their eyeballs down into their heads to push food down their throats.

title: Puffed up
context: A round body bristling with spines, like a balloon covered in pins.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A round fish body covered in long spines.

hints: It's a fish.
It blows itself up to scare off predators.
why: An X-ray of a porcupinefish from the Smithsonian collection, puffed up with its spines sticking out.
pearl: Porcupinefish puff up by gulping water. When inflated, their spines stand on end.

title: Brand new
context: A tiny curled-up mammal, X-rayed in 1896 when it was only just born.
question: What is it?

img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: A small curled mammal skeleton, side on.

hints: Its parents have long ears.
Babies of this animal are called kittens.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a newborn rabbit from the Eder and Valenta portfolio.
pearl: Baby rabbits, called kittens or kits, are born blind and without fur. Their eyes open after about ten days.

title: Upside down
context: A school of thin, pointy fish lined up like pencils.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: Many thin, pointed fish lined up diagonally.

hints: They swim head-down.
Their bodies are encased in thin see-through plates.
why: An X-ray of a group of grooved razorfish (shrimpfish) from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Shrimpfish swim head-down in tight groups, hiding among sea urchin spines and seagrass.

title: Reef picker
context: A deep-bodied reef fish with a snout like a pair of tweezers.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A fish skeleton with a long thin snout and tall fins.

hints: It lives on coral reefs.
It's named after a winged insect.
why: An X-ray of a longnose butterflyfish from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: The longnose butterflyfish uses its tweezer-like snout to pick tiny animals out of cracks in coral.

title: Walking dinner plate
context: A flat, round fish with a short tail and arm-like fins.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A flat round fish with a short tail and arm-like fins.

hints: It walks along the sea floor on its fins.
It shares its name with a breakfast food.
why: An X-ray of a pancake batfish from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Batfish are poor swimmers. They 'walk' across the sea floor on their stiff, leg-like fins.

title: Spiral staircase
context: A perfect curl divided into chamber after chamber.
question: What is it?

img.author: Michel Royon
img.alt: A spiral shell sliced open, showing curved walls dividing it into chambers.

hints: Its owner has tentacles.
It's related to octopus and squid.
why: A CT scan slice through a nautilus shell, showing its spiral of gas-filled chambers.
pearl: A nautilus lives only in the newest, biggest chamber. It adjusts gas and liquid in the older chambers to float up or sink, like a submarine.

title: Pocket-sized
context: A rectangle packed with circuits, a big dark block and lots of tiny parts.
question: What is it?

img.file: Nokia N97 X-ray image Dage XD7500.jpg
img.author: Ossewa
img.alt: A rectangular device with a dark battery block and a grid of circuitry.

hints: It's probably within reach right now.
The big dark block is its battery.
why: An X-ray of a mobile phone: the battery, circuit board, camera and buttons all show up.
pearl: Factories X-ray electronics like this to check for hidden faults in solder joints without opening them up.

title: No legs
context: A long, legless body curving through the picture. It's not what you think.
question: What is it?

img.author: Kalumet
img.alt: A long, legless, curving skeleton on a dark background.

hints: It's an amphibian.
Its closest relatives have legs and croak.
why: An X-ray of a caecilian, a legless amphibian.
pearl: Caecilians are legless amphibians, more closely related to frogs than to snakes or worms. Most live hidden underground.

title: Fresh water
context: A sleek fish built for fast, cold rivers.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A long streamlined fish skeleton.

hints: It's a favourite of fly fishers.
This species is named after the colours along its side.
why: An X-ray of a rainbow trout from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Rainbow trout and steelhead are the same species. Steelhead are the ones that swim out to sea and come back to rivers to breed.

title: Lunchtime
context: A coiled reptile with a bigger bulge than usual near its head. X-rayed in 1896.
question: What is it?

img.file: A snake in the process of swallowing a small mammal, probabl Wellcome V0029552.jpg
img.author: Arthur Schuster (1896), Wellcome Collection
img.alt: A coiled snake skeleton with a small mammal skeleton inside near its head.

hints: Look at the bulge near the head.
Someone small is on the menu.
why: An 1896 X-ray by physicist Arthur Schuster of a snake partway through swallowing a small mammal, probably a mouse.
pearl: Snakes don't really unhinge their jaws. The two halves of the lower jaw are joined by a stretchy ligament, so they can spread apart.

title: Sound the horn
context: A big spiral shell, glowing blue in an X-ray.
question: What is it?

img.author: Michel Royon
img.alt: A large spiral shell shown in blue tones.

hints: People have blown it like a trumpet for centuries.
The animal inside eats a coral-wrecking starfish.
why: An X-ray of the shell of a triton, a large sea snail.
pearl: Giant triton snails are one of the few animals that eat crown-of-thorns starfish, which damage coral reefs.

title: Back from the dead
context: A chunky fish with fleshy, limb-like fins. It was once known only from fossils.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A long, heavy fish skeleton with lobed fins.

hints: It was thought extinct for millions of years.
A museum curator in South Africa recognised one in 1938.
why: An X-ray of a coelacanth from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Coelacanths were thought to have died out with the dinosaurs until museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted one in a fishing catch in 1938.

title: Curly tail
context: A horse-shaped head on top of a coiled tail, ringed with bony plates.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A seahorse skeleton with a horse-like head and a curled tail.

hints: It's a fish, believe it or not.
Dads carry the babies.
why: An X-ray of a seahorse from the Smithsonian's fish collection, showing its bony armour rings.
pearl: In seahorses the male gets pregnant. He carries the eggs in a pouch on his belly until they hatch.
